articles.description: On the frontlines of healthcare, and the strategy table. A cool July afternoon at the Wellcome Collection with the Zimbabwean-British doctor and founder of the women's-health venture Glacie Health, on calling, on education as a form of medicine, and on carrying what the West knows back home to the women who need it.

articles.title: Zimbabwe's tobacco anchor in Britain holds at £129m
articles.description: Of every £100 of goods Zimbabwe sells to Britain, £96 is tobacco or beverages. While the wider UK–Zimbabwe trade relationship softened in the year to December 2025, Zimbabwean tobacco held its grip, and the IMF projects Zimbabwean GDP growth of 7.5% in 2025 and 5.0% in 2026. The product that built Zimbabwe's name as an exporter is still doing the work.

more.title: The Apple of haircare gets its German cheque
more.description: Ruka, the London-based textured-hair company founded by Zimbabwean entrepreneur Varaidzo Tendai Moyo and her co-founder Ugorji Agbai, has closed a $4.5m round co-led by Henkel Ventures and Freedom Trail Capital. The deal, which takes lifetime funding to roughly $10m and brings one of the world's largest consumer-goods groups onto the cap table, is the most meaningful endorsement yet of a Zimbabwean diaspora-founded brand.

more.title: Pardon Mapondera: gone but not forgotten at Venice
more.description: The fifth and final piece in our series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Pardon Mapondera, the artist whose practice the room finally arranges itself around, treats discarded plastic and glass jars not as ecological signal but as ritual matter, and produces, in the process, the most quietly devotional installation in the Biennale this year.

more.title: Gideon Gomo: from stone to bronze, the ancestral algorithm at Venice
more.description: The fourth in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Gideon Gomo's first sustained body of bronze work, paired with discarded vehicle number plates and Zimbabwean springstone, is the move of a sculptor at full maturity rethinking the material vocabulary of his country's most internationally legible art form.

more.title: Shumba Maasai in Venice
more.description: At the 61st Biennale, the Zimbabwean artist's day-long procession through the city's campi, performed under the borrowed authority of a Murehwa chief, restages the social-sculpture lineage of Joseph Beuys for a contemporary African discursive practice.

more.title: Franklyn Dzingai: family albums and the neural commons at Venice
more.description: The third in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Franklyn Dzingai's reductive cardboard prints, built from the family album, the magazine clipping, the back-room studio photographs of mid-century Zimbabwe, turn out, on close looking, to be the most precisely engineered work in the room.

more.title: Felix Shumba: charcoal and the practice of disappearance at Venice
more.description: The second in a five-part series on Zimbabwe's pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale. Felix Shumba's six-metre charcoal wall and his Telephone Reader series anchor a body of work that argues drawing is not the act of capturing the seen, but the act of staying present to what is on its way out of sight.

more.title: UK services share in Zimbabwe rises to 8.2%
more.description: The headline UK services trade with Zimbabwe softened year on year. The structural number underneath it tells the better story: Britain's share of all services Zimbabwe imports rose 2.4 percentage points to 8.2%, the highest measured level in years. As Zimbabwean buyers re-rate their global supplier mix, the UK is taking a bigger slice of the country's services demand.

more.title: Zimbabwe's demand lifts British exports by 14.6%
more.description: The Zimbabwean economy is in its strongest stretch in years: 7.5% GDP growth in 2025, a projected 5% in 2026, and that growth is pulling demand for cars, commercial vehicles, medicines and industrial machinery in with it. UK goods exports to Zimbabwe rose 14.6% on the year, the strongest line in an otherwise soft bilateral picture for Britain.

more.title: First Lady invited to help shape Eurasian Women’s Forum agenda
more.description: Blessings Chidakwa in MOSCOW, Russia FIRST LADY Dr Auxillia Mnangagwa has met the chairperson of the Federation Council of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation, Madame Valentina Matviyenko, who invited her here to contribute ideas and perspectives to discussions for next year’s Eurasian Women’s Forum. The two sisters, united by their shared passion as mothers to uplift women and underserved communities, exchanged perspectives and explored opportunities for cooperation that can benefit women from both nations, including through the Russia-Africa Summit. The invitation, which comes in recognition of Dr Mnangagwa’s sustained work in empowering women and communities, was extended during a heart-to-heart meeting as the two exchanged ideas on programmes that could benefit women and families across continents. The discussions centred on how women can be encouraged to work, develop enterprises, become economically independent and use their skills to improve the welfare of their families and communities. The meeting has been earmarked to unlock opportunities for women’s economic empowerment, cultural exchange and climate-smart agriculture, while strengthening Africa-Europe people-to-people ties through gastronomy, culture, agriculture, education and other collaborative programmes. Dr Mnangagwa, who is also leading a delegation of women from Zimbabwe Legacy Empowerment from all walks of life, said such platforms could enable Zimbabwean women to showcase their talents while learning from experiences in other countries. Zimbabwe’s gastronomy emerged as one area with potential to drive cultural exchange, with traditional food, culinary skills and indigenous products providing a bridge between communities and countries. The idea is to use gastronomy not only to showcase Zimbabwe’s rich cultural heritage, but also to create low-hanging economic opportunities for women in agriculture, food processing, hospitality and tourism. It could also inspire women across Africa to turn their own cultural heritage into economic assets while promoting greater understanding between African and European communities. The discussions further placed women’s economic empowerment within the broader challenge of gender-based violence, with economic independence seen as an important pathway towards strengthening women’s dignity, confidence and ability to make choices about their lives. Madame Matviyenko, who was delighted to warmly receive her sister, Dr Mnangagwa, at the Federation Council, described her as her “dear sister” as they discussed initiatives aimed at improving livelihoods. She then welcomed Dr Mnangagwa’s participation in the upcoming Eurasian Women’s Forum, saying the platform would provide opportunities to promote women’s initiatives and strengthen networks among women. “Your Excellency, Dr Mnangagwa, it is my sincere pleasure that this is our fourth meeting, and for us, it is always a joyous occasion. We have a lot to talk about, to discuss ideas, to outline new plans, and of course we will touch upon the bilateral agenda, on the subjects that unite our countries, especially on the Russia-Africa agenda, as well as the agenda on promoting female initiatives, including the preparation for the upcoming Eurasian Women’s Forum, of which you are also a member. Ever since our first meeting in 2021, when you visited St Petersburg for the Russian Women’s Forum, we have established open, trustworthy relations,” she said. Madame Matviyenko said she was delighted to welcome Dr Mnangagwa for their fourth meeting, describing their encounters as a “joyous occasion” during which they could exchange ideas and “outline new plans”. The Moscow meeting came as Zimbabwe continues to position its women’s empowerment programmes within broader international partnerships, allowing beneficiaries to connect with knowledge, technology, markets and investment opportunities beyond the country’s borders. Madame Matviyenko also expressed hope that President Mnangagwa would visit Russia this year after receiving an invitation, saying she looked forward to his participation in the third Russia-Africa Summit scheduled for October 28 and 29 in Moscow. “We hope that His Excellency, the President, will have the opportunity to lead the representative delegation of Zimbabwe,” she said, adding that the summit would give “a powerful impetus” to cooperation between Russia and Africa. The First Lady started by thanking Madame Matviyenko for their cordial sister-to-sister working relationship, applauding her for visiting Zimbabwe, where she witnessed first-hand the fruits of her Angel of Hope Foundation. Dr Mnangagwa said women needed practical opportunities to work, acquire skills, establish businesses and participate meaningfully in the economy. “Women must be empowered to participate meaningfully in productive economic activities so that they can achieve food security and economic independence,” she said. The First Lady said Zimbabwe had developed several programmes to support women and young people in productive economic activities, particularly agriculture. Through Agric4She, Pfumvudza4She, Poultry4She and Fisheries4She, thousands of beneficiaries have been encouraged to participate in agriculture, improve food security and develop sustainable livelihoods. With climate change increasingly threatening agricultural production, Dr Mnangagwa said African women should make greater use of such programmes while adopting climate-smart approaches to protect their livelihoods. She said agriculture remained one of the most accessible pathways through which rural women could generate income, build enterprises and contribute to the development of their communities. “I would welcome the opportunity to collaborate with Russian parliamentary and regional expertise on rural development, agribusiness value chains and cooperative models that could further benefit our smallholder farmers,” she said. Dr Mnangagwa said her empowerment agenda also extended into the renewable energy sector through Solar4She, which is promoting women’s participation in solar energy. The initiative includes the Gender Assessment Toolkit and the Solar Technology and Application Resource Centre at Chinhoyi University of Technology, providing opportunities for women to gain skills and participate in an emerging sector. She said international partnerships could help women move further up the value chain, expand their enterprises and unlock markets, technology and investment. The First Lady also invited Madame Matviyenko and Russian women leaders to visit Zimbabwe for a reciprocal engagement, where they would meet beneficiaries of the country’s empowerment programmes and exchange experiences with women on the ground. “I, therefore, extend a warm invitation to Russian women leaders, senators and other relevant stakeholders to visit Zimbabwe and engage directly with the beneficiaries of the initiatives I have described,” she said. The reciprocal visit would allow Russian women to see first-hand how programmes such as Agric4She and Solar4She are being implemented, while giving Zimbabwean women an opportunity to learn from Russian experiences. It would also provide an opportunity for the Russian delegation to experience Zimbabwe’s gastronomy, culture and tourism products, further strengthening people-to-people relations between the two countries. Dr Mnangagwa said stronger people-to-people relations could also be built through student exchanges, cultural programmes, media cooperation and training initiatives. She said gastronomy could become an important component of that exchange, particularly as Zimbabwe seeks to use its rich culinary heritage to promote tourism and create economic opportunities for women. Dr Mnangagwa said Zimbabwe’s experience could also provide lessons for women elsewhere, particularly through programmes that combine agriculture, enterprise development, culture and community empowerment. The First Lady’s delegation to Russia is showcasing Zimbabwe’s gastronomy, tourism products and destinations, demonstrating how culture can be transformed into an economic opportunity. The engagement further reflected the longstanding friendship between Dr Mnangagwa and Madame Matviyenko, rooted in their shared interest in families, women, young people and vulnerable communities. Dr Mnangagwa said Zimbabwe valued Russia’s continued support for the country’s development agenda and welcomed opportunities for women from the two countries to share experiences, build networks and strengthen enterprises. “I wish to express my sincere gratitude for Russia’s consistent support of Zimbabwe’s development agenda, and for the warm hospitality always extended to Zimbabwean delegations visiting your great country,” she said. As preparations for next year’s Eurasian Women’s Forum take shape, the Moscow discussions provide an opportunity for Zimbabwe to bring its experience in women’s empowerment, agriculture, renewable energy, gastronomy and community development into a wider conversation on Africa-Europe cooperation. For Dr Mnangagwa, the objective is not simply to expose women to international opportunities, but to ensure they can turn their skills, culture and available resources into viable enterprises that support families, create employment and strengthen communities.

more.title: COMMENT: Evidence suggests Zim’s recovery and growth are now irrepressible
more.description: THE record export figures for the first seven months of 2026 are not a fluke. They are the clearest evidence yet that Zimbabwe’s deliberate pro-business policies, pursued consistently since the advent of the Second Republic, are bearing tangible fruit. Merchandise export earnings surged to US$4,75 billion, up from the figure recorded in the same period last year. Crucially, this growth comfortably outstripped the 31,6 percent rise in imports, swinging Zimbabwe’s trade balance from a deficit of US$799,5 million to a surplus of US$65,6 million. This represents a fundamental structural shift in Zimbabwe’s economic trajectory. At the heart of this transformation lies the US$500 million per year in avoided steel imports. Industrial engineering exports have doubled, soaring 110,4 percent to US$43,1 million in export value — from zero exports in the previous year. Yet what makes this recovery truly irrepressible is the recognition that Manhize remains, by all measures, a fledgling steel plant, with full annual production targeted at 1,2 million tonnes. Dinson is already weighing a threefold output surge to two million tonnes annually. As the plant continues to expand, so, too, will its multiplier effects — on employment, on downstream industries like cement production and on regional market penetration. With approximately 60 percent of the current output already being exported to the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region, Zimbabwe is decisively shifting from a net importer of steel to a regional producer and exporter. Manhize, however, is but one node in a rapidly expanding network of transformative investments unfolding across the country. In Beitbridge, the US$3,6 billion Xintai Palm River Energy and Metallurgical Industrial Park is taking shape, spanning 5 100 hectares within a special economic zone. The project encompasses a coking plant with annual capacity of one million tonnes, a ferro-chrome smelting plant producing 100 000 tonnes of high-carbon ferro-chrome and a 1 200-megawatt coal-fired thermal power plant. Upon completion, it will employ over 2 000 people and substantially contribute to Zimbabwe’s mining and energy sectors. These are not isolated projects but interconnected pillars of a deliberate industrialisation strategy under the National Development Strategy 2 (NDS2). Parallel to this industrial boom, Zimbabwe’s bilateral trade with China has also increased, with blueberries nearly doubling to US$8,5 million. This is the dividend of economic diplomacy and the “open for business” mantra that has defined the Second Republic’s engagement and re-engagement agenda. Market watchers are now increasingly betting on Zimbabwe’s phenomenal growth in the medium to long term — and for good reason. The macroeconomic foundation has never been more stable. Inflation has fallen from a peak of 95,8 percent in July 2025 to single-digit levels in 2026, averaging 4,2 percent in the first seven months — the first time in over 30 years that the country has recorded sustained single-digit inflation. The economy grew by 8,3 percent in 2025 and is projected to expand by approximately 5 percent this year. Critics may point to lingering risks, and indeed, global headwinds remain. But the evidence of the past several years — continued investments across mining, manufacturing, energy and agriculture, sustained macroeconomic stability and a consistent policy framework — is the clearest sign yet that Zimbabwe is on the rise. The Second Republic laid the policy foundation. The private sector, both domestic and international, is building upon it. What was once dismissed as ambition is now manifesting as achievement. As Manhize expands, as Palm River comes online, as value addition and beneficiation take root across the economy, Zimbabwe is not merely recovering — it is transforming. The country is, in all likelihood, on course to achieve its lofty aspirations under Vision 2030. The recovery and growth are now irrepressible.
